title: Frontend Architecture: Module Boundaries and Refactoring
description: Design dependency direction, assign state ownership, refactor duplicated behavior and make errors recoverable.
learningOutcomes: Define module boundaries around responsibilities and reasons to change.
Explain import direction and recognize circular dependencies.
Assign URL, server, shared and local UI state to suitable owners.
Refactor duplication behind a stable contract without building unnecessary abstractions.
Design consistent error states and repeatable verification.
Apply SOLID principles when they reduce a concrete coupling or change-cost problem without overengineering.

blocks.text: Architecture is the shape of change

A useful architecture helps a developer find the behavior they need to change, understand which layer owns it, and verify the result. A module should have a coherent responsibility and a clear public interface. Folder names alone do not create architecture: dependency direction, data ownership and testing boundaries matter more than whether a project uses a particular folder template.

blocks.code:
Route / page
  -> Feature orchestration
      -> Custom Hook / state transition
          -> Service / API contract
      -> UI components (props in, callbacks out)
Shared primitives and tokens <- feature UI

Avoid these reverse edges:
UI primitive -> route page
Service -> React component
Feature A <-> Feature B circular imports

steps.title: Keep orchestration close to a user journey
steps.explanation: The route composes a feature and the feature coordinates the workflow. A custom Hook can own reusable lifecycle/state behavior without turning every function into a Hook.

steps.title: Keep service and presentation contracts separate
steps.explanation: A service knows the transport/data contract; a UI component renders values and emits events. Components do not need to know HTTP details, and the service does not need to import JSX.

steps.title: Shared dependencies should stay lower-level
steps.explanation: UI primitives can be consumed by features, but importing route pages back into a primitive creates a reverse dependency. Mutual imports between features make changes and tests harder to isolate.

items: Group files by a feature when they change together; group by technical type when the application is small and the shared layer is still clear. Neither convention is universal.
A module boundary should reflect a reason to change, a stable contract, or an independently testable responsibility—not simply a file count.
Keep URL state for shareable/filterable navigation, server state near its data-fetching/cache boundary, and transient interaction state local unless multiple consumers need a shared owner.
Refactor in small steps: characterize current behavior with tests, introduce a seam, move one responsibility, run checks, then remove duplication.
An error boundary catches rendering failures, while request errors and form errors need their own explicit states. One generic try/catch is not an error strategy for every layer.

blocks.prompt: Which dependency direction best fits a reusable Button component in a layered frontend application?

options.text: The Button imports the route page to know when it should render
options.feedback: A low-level UI primitive should not depend on an application route. The page should compose the Button.

options.text: Feature UI imports the shared Button and passes props/callbacks
options.feedback: This keeps the shared primitive lower-level and lets the feature own the user journey.

options.text: The API service imports Button and displays HTTP errors directly
options.feedback: A service should return a clear result/error contract; presentation belongs to the UI layer.

options.text: Two features import each other to share state implicitly
options.feedback: Mutual imports create circular dependencies and obscure state ownership.

blocks.explanation: Dependency direction should make lower-level modules reusable and keep responsibilities explicit.

blocks.title: Refactor a tightly coupled feature into clear boundaries
blocks.context: Given a page that fetches data, validates responses, renders forms and shares helper logic through circular imports, propose and implement a safer boundary.
instructions: Draw the current dependency graph and mark any circular imports.
Move HTTP/status parsing into a service contract and map its outcomes into explicit UI states.
Choose owners for URL filters, server data and transient modal state.
Extract one repeated UI behavior behind a small reusable contract, keeping the feature-specific decisions in the feature.
Define tests that protect current behavior before and after the refactor.
requirements: The dependency graph has a clear direction and no feature-to-feature cycle.
HTTP concerns and presentation concerns have separate interfaces.
State ownership matches sharing and persistence requirements.
The abstraction is justified by reuse or a stable contract, not created only to reduce line count.
Tests cover success, empty and error/recovery behavior.
hints: Start by identifying which layer has the authority to decide each behavior.
If a value should survive refresh and be shared by link, consider URL state.
Refactor one seam at a time so a failing test localizes the change.
successCriteria: A target dependency graph is documented.
State owners and layer interfaces are explicit.
Circular imports are removed or justified with a better boundary.
Behavior-preserving and failure-state tests are listed.

blocks.text: Choose a structure from the change pattern

Folder structure is a coordination tool, not a score of architectural maturity. A small app with a few screens may stay understandable with a flat or layer-oriented layout. As features grow, feature-based folders help keep UI, model and API work that changes together nearby. Larger teams may add explicit domain boundaries or a documented feature-layer convention. Move to a more restrictive structure when recurring navigation, dependency or ownership problems justify its cost—not because a diagram is fashionable.

items: Flat by technical type (components/, hooks/, services/) is easy to start and search; it can become hard to tell which files form one feature.
Feature-oriented folders improve change locality and ownership; shared UI should be promoted only when more than one feature truly needs the same stable behavior.
Layered or domain-oriented boundaries make dependency rules visible, but extra interfaces and folders can slow a small app if they do not isolate a real reason to change.
Barrel exports simplify imports but may hide cycles or pull in more code than expected; prefer explicit public entry points and verify the actual bundle when size matters.

blocks.code:
src/
  app/
    routes/
  features/
    billing/
      api/
      model/
      ui/
      index.ts
    profile/
      api/
      model/
      ui/
  shared/
    ui/
    lib/
    styles/

steps.title: Keep feature-owned behavior together
steps.explanation: The feature folder groups files that change for one user capability. The internal folders are optional; do not add every subfolder before the feature needs separate responsibilities.

steps.title: Keep shared code below the features that use it
steps.explanation: Shared UI and utilities should not import billing or profile. If a common helper starts importing feature policy, it is not truly shared; move the policy to a feature or define a deliberate contract.

blocks.text: Colocate related files and expose a small public API

Colocation puts files that tend to change together—component, styles, tests, local Hook and domain types—near each other. A feature's `index.ts` can be its public entry point, so consumers do not depend on internal file layout. Choose folders by responsibility and change locality; not every module needs every subfolder.

steps.title: Notice change locality
steps.explanation: Before refactoring, tests, styles and Hook code for one component are scattered across technical folders. This makes it harder to find the complete change surface and may leave orphan files.

steps.title: Colocate related implementation files
steps.explanation: Keep files that usually change together inside a feature-oriented folder. Internal folders are optional: use them only when they improve separation, not just to follow a template.

steps.title: Expose an intentional public API
steps.explanation: An explicit index.ts keeps the supported export surface small. A barrel does not make other files private by itself, and wildcard re-exports can accidentally expand that surface or hide cycles.

steps.title: Use the contract from outside
steps.explanation: Consumers use the public entry point. If deep imports must be prohibited, add a lint/import-boundary rule; do not assume the folder convention is enforced automatically.

blocks.text: The source's “rule of three” is a heuristic, not a law: duplicated code can remain local while consumers differ, and extraction makes sense when repeated use reveals a stable contract. Prefer composition over a component with many unrelated boolean props. Promote code to shared only when its behavior is genuinely domain-neutral; the number of copies is evidence to inspect, not an automatic refactor trigger.

blocks.prompt: A feature's `index.ts` currently re-exports every internal module, and consumers import private file paths directly. Which change best improves the boundary without overengineering?

options.text: Move all feature files into shared and use export * so every consumer can reach them
options.feedback: Feature-specific rules do not become shared just because several modules import them; wildcard exports also broaden the public surface.

options.text: Colocate files that change together, export only supported symbols, and enforce public-entry imports if the rule must be strict
options.feedback: A small explicit API documents the contract; colocation helps navigation, while lint rules can enforce import boundaries when needed.

options.text: Create a separate package and interface for every file before changing any imports
options.feedback: Extra packages and interfaces create migration and maintenance cost without proving that each file needs an independent boundary.

options.text: Keep all imports as they are because an index.ts file automatically makes other paths inaccessible
options.feedback: A TypeScript barrel is not an access-control mechanism; deep imports remain possible unless project tooling forbids them.

blocks.explanation: Colocation describes where related files live. A public API describes which symbols other modules are expected to consume. Neither convention alone enforces private paths, so use lint boundaries when strict enforcement matters.

blocks.title: Refactor a feature folder and define its public API
blocks.context: A ProductCard feature has its component, styles, Hook and tests scattered across type-based folders. Another screen imports the component through a private implementation path. The catalog and saved-lessons cards look similar but still have different behavior.
instructions: Draw a colocated target tree for the component, style, Hook, test and any domain types that change with ProductCard.
Write an explicit index.ts export list for the supported component and public types; keep internal helpers out unless consumers need them.
Rewrite the consumer import to use the public module entry point and explain how lint can prevent future deep imports.
Decide whether the catalog and saved-lessons cards should remain separate or share a primitive; justify the decision by behavior and contract, not file count alone.
List characterization tests and an import-cycle check to run before and after the refactor.
requirements: Groups files by change locality without putting domain-specific logic into shared automatically.
Defines a minimal, explicit index.ts public API.
Updates consumers to import via the public entry point.
Explains that lint/import-boundary rules are needed to enforce deep-import restrictions.
Documents the trade-off behind sharing or keeping similar card components local.
Preserves visible behavior with tests and checks for circular dependencies.

blocks.text: A boundary is useful when callers can use a small contract without knowing implementation details. For example, a page can ask a feature to load a billing summary; the feature can call a service that returns typed data. Keep HTTP parsing outside presentational components and map transport failures into results the feature can explain. Do not create interfaces for every function: introduce a seam when it supports reuse, independent testing, or a change that otherwise crosses unrelated modules.

blocks.code:
Problem:
Route -> Feature -> shared/UI
shared/UI -> Route       // reverse dependency
Feature A <-> Feature B  // import cycle

Safer direction:
Route -> Feature
Feature -> shared/UI
Feature -> BillingService contract
BillingService -> HTTP adapter

steps.title: Locate the cycle instead of blaming folders
steps.explanation: A shared button reaching back into a route couples low-level rendering to one screen. Two features importing each other make change and test order unpredictable.

steps.title: Keep the caller facing a small contract
steps.explanation: The route composes a feature; the feature may use stable shared primitives and a service contract. The HTTP adapter owns request and response parsing. This is a useful direction, not a mandate to build a generic dependency-injection framework.

blocks.prompt: Two product features each import the other's state helpers, and changing either feature frequently breaks the other. What is the best first architectural move?

options.text: Move every file into a new framework before tracing the dependency
options.feedback: A large reorganization does not explain which behavior is coupled and can create more migration risk.

options.text: Draw the import graph, identify the shared rule or contract, and remove one cycle in a tested step
options.feedback: First make the dependency and reason for change visible; then choose the smallest boundary that breaks the cycle without changing behavior.

options.text: Add a barrel file to each feature so the circular imports are shorter
options.feedback: Barrels may shorten syntax but do not remove a cycle; they can make import relationships less obvious.

options.text: Copy both helpers into every caller so no one imports either feature
options.feedback: Copying may hide the cycle temporarily but creates drift and duplicate behavior that must be reconciled later.

blocks.explanation: Architecture work starts with evidence about change and dependency direction. Characterization tests and a small seam make the refactor reversible.

blocks.text: Place state where its lifetime and consumers require

Choose a state owner by asking who must read it, how long it must survive, and whether it belongs in a URL, server response or local interaction. Search filters that should survive refresh and be shareable often belong in URL parameters. Remote records belong to a request/cache boundary with loading, empty, error and refresh behavior. A temporary open dialog can stay local. Do not move all state into Context or global storage merely because several components exist; lift it only to the nearest owner that actually coordinates those consumers.

blocks.prompt: A filtered catalog should be shareable as a link and restored after refresh. Which owner is usually the strongest starting point?

options.text: A local boolean in the filter button
options.feedback: Local component state disappears on refresh and cannot be encoded in a link.

options.text: URL query parameters, parsed and validated by the route or feature
options.feedback: The URL is addressable, shareable and participates in browser navigation; the feature should still validate values and define defaults.

options.text: A global Context that stores every page's filter
options.feedback: Global state can outlive or couple unrelated pages and does not automatically provide a shareable URL.

options.text: A module-level variable
options.feedback: A module variable is not a durable or navigable source of state and can be shared unexpectedly.

blocks.explanation: State placement follows lifetime, sharing and recovery needs—not component count alone.

blocks.title: Choose boundaries for a growing catalog feature
blocks.context: A small course catalog has URL filters, server-fetched courses, a temporary enrollment dialog and two screens that share a search field. The current feature imports route code in both directions and keeps request parsing in a button component.
instructions: Draw the current dependency graph and mark the reverse edge or cycle.
Choose a URL owner for shareable filters, a request/cache owner for course data, and a local owner for the temporary dialog.
Propose a target folder or module map that fits a small team today; note one signal that would justify splitting a new module later.
Define a narrow service/result contract and state how network, empty and validation failures reach the UI.
Plan characterization and focused tests for navigation, request outcomes and enrollment dialog behavior.
requirements: The target graph has one deliberate direction and no feature-to-feature cycle.
Shareable filters, remote data and transient interaction state have different owners.
The proposed abstraction solves a stated change/testing problem and avoids speculative layering.
Tests protect observable behavior and include a failure/recovery path.

blocks.text: Apply SOLID as design questions, not a mandatory checklist

SOLID names five principles that can help when responsibilities or dependencies make change expensive. They are prompts for examining a design—not a requirement to create an interface, factory, repository, service and Hook for every component. Start from a concrete change, testability problem or dependency that is hard to replace; introduce only the boundary that addresses it.

items: Single Responsibility (SRP): group behavior around one coherent reason to change. A component may render a form, while a feature function coordinates submission and a service owns HTTP details; “one responsibility” does not mean one line or one method.

Open/Closed (OCP): let stable behavior be extended through an intentional variant, mapping or strategy when new cases repeatedly force edits in many branches. It does not mean existing code must never change or every possible future variant needs an extension point.

Liskov Substitution (LSP): an implementation that satisfies a contract should preserve its documented behavior and result/error expectations. A mock, cache adapter and HTTP implementation should not silently promise different semantics for the same operation.

Interface Segregation (ISP): give a consumer the small capability it needs instead of a broad object containing unrelated actions. Separate narrow contracts when they have different consumers/reasons to change, not merely to maximise the number of types.

Dependency Inversion (DIP): high-level feature logic should depend on a stable contract rather than embedding a particular transport or concrete service. Pass a function or service contract when that seam enables replacement or testing; dependency injection is a technique, not an end in itself.

steps.title: Make operation contracts explicit
steps.explanation: The result union makes success and expected validation/network failure explicit. SaveOrder and SendReceipt are narrow capabilities rather than one broad service object.

steps.title: Keep orchestration separate from transport
steps.explanation: submitOrder coordinates the workflow through injected operations. It can be tested with controlled implementations without knowing whether saving uses fetch, Axios or a local test adapter.

steps.title: Keep the UI focused on presentation
steps.explanation: OrderSummary renders an order and emits an action. It does not parse HTTP, send email or own analytics; the feature can coordinate those side effects and report status.

options.text: Identify the reasons to change, move transport/orchestration to focused contracts, and keep the component responsible for its UI
options.feedback: A small refactor separates responsibilities and allows the workflow to be tested without the browser or live HTTP/email dependencies.

options.text: Create a separate package, interface and factory for every function before writing tests
options.feedback: SOLID does not prescribe a fixed number of layers; speculative abstractions can increase the cost of every change.

options.text: Keep every side effect in the component because one file is easier to find
options.feedback: Colocation can help navigation, but it does not separate transport failures, workflow rules and visual presentation.

options.text: Replace the component with a generic base class and prohibit future edits to it
options.feedback: OCP is not a ban on changing code. Choose a stable extension point only when a concrete variation justifies it.

blocks.explanation: Apply a principle to an observed change or testing problem. Start with one boundary that lowers coupling, and keep the change small enough to verify.

blocks.title: Refactor one feature seam using a SOLID principle
blocks.context: An order component currently renders a form, parses HTTP JSON, selects a validation message, sends a receipt email and tracks analytics. A new payment adapter is being added, and tests require a live API to cover the flow.
instructions: Draw the current dependency/reason-to-change map and identify the specific behavior that changes for the payment-adapter requirement.
Choose one or two relevant principles (SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP) and explain why they fit the observed problem rather than applying all five mechanically.
Extract one small contract or function so the UI renders and emits actions while feature orchestration owns the workflow and the service owns transport parsing.
Define success and expected failure results; keep adapter implementations consistent with the documented contract.
Write the smallest useful tests that exercise the workflow with controlled implementations and preserve existing user-visible behavior.
requirements: The selected principle is tied to a concrete reason to change or a testability problem.
The new dependency direction is explicit and has no reverse import/cycle.
The component does not own unrelated HTTP, email and analytics implementation details.
Success and expected error outcomes are documented in a small contract.
The design does not add a generic layer or extension point without a stated consumer need.
The plan includes tests for success and at least one expected failure while preserving behavior.
hints: Ask which requirement or actor causes this code to change; that is more useful than counting lines in a component.
A narrow function type can be enough for dependency inversion in a small React feature; a class/interface/factory is not always required.
Keep the success/error contract consistent for real, mock and test implementations, and test observable outcomes at the feature boundary.
successCriteria: The refactor explains one concrete reason to change and names the principle it addresses.
UI rendering and side-effect orchestration have a clear boundary.
Dependencies can be replaced in tests without using a live network/email service.
The contract describes success and expected failure consistently.
The solution avoids speculative layers and preserves existing behavior with tests.

blocks.text: Choose ecosystem tools by the responsibility they own

items: Routing: React Router maps URLs to views; follow the version already installed in the project and keep shareable navigation in the URL.

Remote data: a service/custom Hook can be enough for a small flow. Consider a query/cache library when caching, deduplication, invalidation and background refresh justify the extra dependency; remote data is not automatically global UI state.
Forms: native or controlled inputs can be enough for simple forms; a form library plus runtime schema validation may help when field state, validation and error handling become complex.

Shared client state: Context or a store such as Zustand can coordinate genuinely shared preferences and actions. Do not move server data into a global client store just because multiple components read it.
UI component systems: compare accessibility semantics, styling/customization, bundle cost and team maintenance. Avoid introducing a second UI system only because a course or article recommends it.
Testing: for a Vite project, Vitest and Testing Library can verify user-visible behavior; prefer accessible, behavior-oriented queries over selectors coupled to private markup.
Architecture helps locate change and verify behavior; folder layout alone does not create it.
Keep dependency direction deliberate and state ownership explicit.
Refactor in small, testable steps and distinguish rendering, request and validation errors.
